title: Why rehearsing beats more reading

beats.say: Would you pass a driving test by reading one more manual?

show.sub: Would it pass the driving test?

beats.say: Reading the rules of the road is not the same as driving with an examiner beside you. Reading builds recognition. Driving builds the skill of staying calm and clear while someone watches and the clock runs.
An interview is the same. By now you have built things and written designs, so the gap is no longer knowledge. The gap is saying it out loud, in order, in forty-five minutes, to a stranger.
So rehearse the real thing. Talk through a design against a timer, get feedback, and go again.

check.q: You already know the material well. What most improves your interview result now?
opts: Reading one more book
Timed, spoken practice with feedback
Waiting until you feel ready
check.why: The remaining gap is performing out loud under time pressure, and only rehearsal in that format closes it.

work: Book a timed 45 minute mock this week.
Explain one design out loud to a colleague without notes.

title: The practice loop that builds skill

beats.say: Why does one mock interview teach more than a week of reading?
Because of a loop. You attempt a problem cold, in forty-five minutes, out loud. Then you review the gaps: where you froze, rambled, or skipped a trade-off.
Pulling an answer from memory strengthens it far more than rereading it. Each failed attempt shows exactly what to fix, and fixing it takes about twenty minutes, not a week.
Repeat it: one timed attempt, one review, one targeted fix. Ten loops beat thirty hours of notes.

check.q: Why does a timed mock find problems that reading does not?
opts: It forces you to retrieve and express answers, exposing gaps
It covers more topics per hour
It removes the need for review
check.why: Retrieving answers under time pressure shows where recall and structure break, which rereading hides.

work: Run one timed attempt, then write three misses within ten minutes.
Fix only the top miss before the next attempt.

title: How practice goes wrong

beats.say: What goes wrong when you practise a lot but still fail the loop?

Three traps. First, practising with no feedback, so you repeat the same mistake ten times. Second, replaying only your strong topics because they feel good. Third, practising relaxed, with no timer and no one watching.

show.title: Three traps
items: No feedback: same mistake ten times
Only strengths: feels good, learns little
No pressure: timer and audience missing

beats.say: Two more. Memorised scripts collapse the moment the interviewer changes one requirement, so practise reacting to interruptions. And cramming a brand new topic the night before only adds anxiety.

show.title: Two more
items: Scripts break when a requirement changes

beats.say: Keep a log of every miss. If the same miss appears three times, it is a pattern, so drill it on purpose.

show.title: Miss log
show.text:
miss: skipped failure modes
seen: 3 times
action: drill on purpose

check.q: The interviewer changes a requirement halfway and your memorised answer falls apart. What is the best fix?
opts: Memorise more scripts
Practise adapting to interruptions and changed constraints
Avoid mocks with interruptions
check.why: Real interviews shift mid-way, so you need to reason from principles and adapt rather than recite.

work: Ask your mock partner to change a requirement midway.
Keep a miss log and flag anything seen three times.

title: Knowing when to stop practising

beats.say: When is practising the wrong move, and more studying the right one?
When a mock exposes a real knowledge gap, like not knowing how exactly-once delivery works. Practising cannot fix what you do not know. Study that one gap, then go back to mocks.
Mocks differ in cost and fidelity. A friend is free but kind. A paid senior interviewer costs more but gives honest, calibrated feedback. Use friends for volume and experts for the last few rounds.
Returns diminish. Once your misses stop repeating, stop, and rest. A sharp mind on the day is worth more than one extra mock.

check.q: Your mock shows you cannot explain a core concept at all. What now?
opts: Do more mocks of the same kind
Study that specific gap briefly, then re-test it in a mock
Stop all preparation
check.why: Practice exposes gaps but cannot create missing knowledge, so close the gap with targeted study, then verify it under pressure.

work: Sort your last misses into knowledge gaps versus delivery gaps.
Use friends for early mocks and book an expert for the final rounds.

title: Why a loop has many interviewers

beats.say: Why would a company make you sit through five or six interviews in a single loop?

Think of a house inspection. One inspector checks the roof, another the wiring, another the plumbing. A loop works the same way. Each interviewer tests one skill, so one weak hour cannot sink you, and one blind spot cannot hide.

For a data engineer, the skills are asking questions of tables with SQL, writing code, shaping data into tidy tables, designing pipelines, and working well with people. Five to seven rounds cover them all.

check.q: Why do companies split a hiring loop into many rounds?
opts: Each round tests a different skill, so no single hour decides everything
To make the process as long as possible
Because every interviewer asks the same question
So candidates can choose the easiest round
check.why: Separate examiners check separate skills, which spreads the risk of one bad hour and exposes blind spots.

work: List the five skill areas a data engineer loop covers and rate yourself on each.
Ask a recruiter which skill each round targets.

title: The shared anatomy of five loops

beats.say: What do five very different company loops have in common?

Round counts are close. Amazon reports up to seven, Meta six, and Uber, Atlassian and Databricks five each. Every single loop includes SQL, usually with window functions. A window function looks at neighbouring rows without collapsing them, like finding last month's value with LAG.

Next comes design: modeling tables for ride sharing or food delivery, or sketching a pipeline for clicks or ads. Last is a behavioral round on ownership and failure. So prepare four pillars: SQL, code, design, and stories.

check.q: Which element appears in all five reported loops?
opts: A SQL round, often with window functions
A Scala coding test
A bar raiser round
A take-home project
check.why: SQL appears in every loop; the bar raiser is Amazon only, Scala is one Databricks report, and take-homes are not universal.

work: Write top N per group, LAG and running total queries from memory.
Draft one modeling answer for ride sharing and one for food delivery.

title: Each company's signature round

beats.say: If every loop has SQL, how do you tell them apart?

By the signature round. Amazon digs into AWS: skew, S3 partitioning and cluster cost, plus a leadership bar raiser. Uber pairs hard SQL with a medium algorithm problem and Spark internals. Meta leans on product metrics, asking what a number means for a new feature.

Atlassian probes Delta schema changes, exactly-once processing and late data. Databricks goes deep on Spark shuffles, Kafka ordering, and privacy rules like GDPR. Same skills, different emphasis, so tune your last week of prep to the company.

check.q: Which pairing matches a reported signature?
opts: Uber: hard SQL plus a medium algorithm problem
Meta: S3 partitioning and EMR cost
Amazon: Kafka ordering and GDPR
Atlassian: ride-hailing SQL only
check.why: Uber pairs hard SQL with a medium DSA problem; S3 and EMR are Amazon, Kafka and GDPR are Databricks.

work: Pick your next target company and list its two signature topics.
Study one signature topic deeply: for example shuffle reduction or exactly-once.

title: Reports age: confirm before you rehearse

beats.say: What is the biggest risk when you prepare from a reported interview loop?

That it is out of date. These are candidate reports, not official descriptions, and loops change. Meta's older reports show separate SQL and modeling rounds. Newer ones describe one combined sitting with product sense mixed in.

Two details can sink you. AI rules: Amazon is reported to treat undisclosed AI use as cheating, while some Meta rounds expect it. And language: one Databricks report lists Scala. Ask the recruiter about format, language and AI before you start.

show.title: Ask the recruiter
items: AI use: banned, disclosed or expected?

check.q: A report says a loop forbids undisclosed AI use. What should you do?
opts: Ask the recruiter for the current AI policy and follow it
Assume every company has the same rule
Use AI quietly if the problem is hard
Ignore it because reports are always wrong
check.why: Policies differ by company and change over time, so confirm directly and disclose if required.

work: Send the recruiter a short list: format, language, AI policy, tools allowed.
Practice once with and once without AI help so you can handle both.

title: Rounds that hide two interviews

beats.say: Why does one interview round often hide two interviews inside it?

Because companies pair skills. Amazon mixes SQL with a clickstream design that must survive ten times the traffic. Uber follows a hard query with a medium algorithm problem on arrays, stacks or binary search. Meta can blend SQL, modeling and product sense.

The failure mode is time. If you spend forty minutes perfecting the query, the second half gets five. Practice finishing SQL in about twenty minutes, state your tie rules for top N per group, then move on and say what you would improve.

show.title: Time discipline
items: Aim for SQL in about twenty minutes
State tie handling for top N

check.q: In a paired SQL plus design round, what is the most common failure?
opts: Running out of time for the second half
Writing the query too fast
Skipping the greeting
Using too many window functions
check.why: Over-polishing the first half leaves too little time for the second, which is graded too.

work: Time yourself on SQL problems and cap each at twenty minutes.
Practice a hard query followed straight away by a design question.

title: Spend prep time like an architect

beats.say: You have three weeks and five different loops. How do you split your time?

Go for the overlap first. SQL windows, data modeling, pipeline design with late data and skew, and behavioral stories show up in all five. Mastering that core covers most of every loop, so give it most of your hours.

Then spend the rest on each signature, in order of your interview dates. Do not learn a language for one report; ask first. And build five reusable stories on failure, ownership and conflict. One story set serves every leadership round.

show.title: Allocate the rest
items: Five stories reused across leadership rounds

check.q: Why prioritise the shared core over any one company's signature topic?
opts: It pays off in every loop, so each hour has the highest return
Signature topics never appear in interviews
Companies only test shared topics
It is easier to study
check.why: Shared skills appear across all loops, so effort there is reused, while signatures help only one company and may be outdated.

work: Split prep roughly 60 percent shared core and 40 percent signatures, then adjust by interview date.
Write five stories on failure, ownership, conflict, influence and a hard trade-off, and map each to every behavioral round.

title: The open kitchen: a repo that proves it

beats.say: Would you hire a chef who only says they can cook, or one who lets you walk into the kitchen?
A project repository is that open kitchen. The first file, called the README, says in one paragraph what the platform does. Then a map of the parts. Then how to run it.
Short notes explain why you picked each tool. A diary of things that broke shows you have really operated it. A table of scores shows how well your helper agent did.

show.title: What else is inside
items: Score table: how the agent did

beats.say: And you say plainly: this is a personal project on made-up data, built to learn. Honesty earns more trust than hype.

check.q: Why does an incident diary help in a portfolio repo?
opts: It makes the repo longer
It shows you have operated what you built, not just built it
It replaces the README
It hides the bugs
check.why: Operating a system means things break. A cleaned-up record of failures and fixes is evidence of real experience.

work: Write your README opening paragraph in plain words so a non-engineer understands it.
Ask a friend to open your repo and say what it does after one minute.

title: The five-minute demo script

beats.say: You get asked, tell me about a project. What do you say in five minutes?
Spend thirty seconds on the problem. Then one minute on the architecture: how data flows from source to table to dashboard.
Give two minutes to the star moment: a live failure. The agent diagnoses it and posts the cause to Slack while the interviewer watches. Watching beats hearing about it.
Then one minute of evaluation numbers: incidents, scores, cost per incident. Finish with thirty seconds on what you would build next. Rehearse three times so it fits.

check.q: Which part of the five-minute demo gets the most time, and why?
opts: Architecture, because diagrams are impressive
The live failure diagnosed by the agent, because showing it working is stronger than describing it
What you build next, because it shows ambition
The problem statement, to set context
check.why: Two minutes go to the live failure and Slack post. Seeing the system work end to end is the most convincing proof.

work: Time yourself running the demo script three times and trim whatever overruns.
Write one sentence per segment so you can hit each time box.

title: When the demo or the questions bite back

beats.say: What happens when your live demo breaks for real, in front of the interviewer?
Plan for it. Inject one known failure, so the same break happens each time. The agent is not deterministic, so also keep a recorded run ready as backup. Say so calmly.

Interviewers probe decisions. Why does the agent only propose fixes? Because a wrong automatic change to production data costs far more than a human click. Each record should name the option you rejected and the price you accepted.
Show misses in the evaluation table too. A table with only perfect scores looks invented.

check.q: Why should the agent only propose fixes rather than apply them?
opts: Proposals are cheaper to compute
A wrong automatic change to production data is costly, and a human approval is cheap
Slack cannot run commands
Agents cannot read logs
check.why: The asymmetry is the point: a human check costs seconds, while a wrong automatic change can corrupt data and take hours to undo.

work: Create a deterministic failure you can trigger on demand and record a backup run of it.
Add a rejected alternative and its cost to each design decision record.
Include at least one incident the agent got wrong in your evaluation table.

title: Presenting limits like an architect

beats.say: Your demo is done. What separates a staff answer from a student answer?

Judgment about limits. Say what synthetic data cannot prove: real volume, messy upstream changes, real users. Then name what you expect to break first at scale, for example many small files in the table, or agent cost growing with incident count.

Cost per incident is your argument. If the agent costs cents and saves a human thirty minutes, automation pays. If it is wrong half the time, it only drafts, which is why it proposes and never applies.

show.title: Cost as an argument
items: Cents per incident versus 30 human minutes

beats.say: Choose next steps from the incident log, not from fashion. Build what failed most often.

check.q: An interviewer asks what you would build next. Which answer shows the strongest judgment?
opts: Adopt the newest tool in the ecosystem
Rebuild everything on a larger cluster
Fix the failure type that appears most in the incident log, with the evaluation numbers as the baseline
Add more dashboards
check.why: Choosing next work from recorded failures and measured results is evidence-driven, and it shows you treat the platform as an operated system.

work: Add a limits section to the README listing what synthetic data cannot show.
Count incidents by type and pick your next feature from the top one.
Compute average agent cost per incident and compare it with the human time saved.

title: A resume is a menu

beats.say: Why would a restaurant menu with fewer dishes win more customers?
A resume is a menu. The reader is hungry and rushed. They spend about thirty seconds deciding. So the first line must say what you cook best.
Every dish you list, the chef must cook live if asked. An interviewer will ask. A dish you cannot cook, such as a skill you only heard of, ruins trust in the whole menu.
So list fewer things, lead with your signature dish, and be ready to explain every one for five minutes.

check.q: Why list fewer skills on a resume?
opts: Short lists look more modern
Every listed item can be tested, and one weak one hurts trust in the rest
Recruiters only read one line
Long lists are rejected by software
check.why: Interviewers probe what you list. A claim you cannot defend damages belief in your strong claims.

work: Highlight every skill on your resume you could not explain for five minutes.
Rewrite the first line so it names your best specialities.

title: Anatomy of a strong resume

beats.say: What does a senior data engineer resume actually contain, top to bottom?

show.sub: Four parts that carry the weight

beats.say: First, the headline. Write Senior Data Engineer, then your strongest specialities, like streaming and warehouse modelling. AI goes in the second line, as the thing that sets you apart.

Second, each role opens with the largest system you worked on and its scale. For example, a pipeline moving two billion events a day for forty analysts. Scale tells the reader your level in one glance.
Third, add a project with a repository link, such as a platform and an on call agent. Then order skills by what you can defend, not by what you have heard of.

show.title: Finish strong
items: Skills ordered by what you can defend

check.q: Where should the largest system and its scale appear?
opts: In a skills list at the bottom
At the start of each role
Only in the headline
Only in the project section
check.why: Opening each role with the biggest system and its scale shows your level immediately.

work: Rewrite each role's first line to name the biggest system and a scale figure.
Reorder skills with the most defensible first.

title: Numbers you must defend

beats.say: You wrote cut latency by sixty percent. What is the first thing an interviewer asks?
They ask how you measured it. Sixty percent from what baseline, over what period, on which dashboard? A number with no baseline is just decoration, and it invites doubt.
Next they ask what you did, versus what others did. Saying we hides your part. Saying I for a team effort gets caught fast. Be exact: I designed the partitioning, a colleague built the loader.

show.title: Split the credit honestly
items: I for a team effort gets caught

beats.say: The same test applies to skills. List Spark and they may ask about shuffles and skew. If you cannot answer, remove it. One weak claim makes the strong ones look doubtful.

check.q: Which resume line is safest in an interview?
opts: Improved performance a lot
Cut p95 query time from 12s to 5s, measured on our dashboard, by redesigning partitioning myself
We rebuilt the whole platform
Expert in ten tools
check.why: It has a baseline, a measure, and a clear personal contribution, so it survives five minutes of questions.

work: For each number, write the baseline, source, your part, and others' parts.
Replace vague we statements with specific I and they statements.

title: Choosing what goes on the page

beats.say: Should your headline say data engineer or AI engineer?

Choose by the role you are applying for. For a data engineering job, lead with data engineering. Data platforms are what they hire for. AI as a second line adds a difference without making them wonder if you want a different job.

The trade-off is breadth against trust. Every extra line costs reader attention and creates one more thing to defend. At staff level, show scope and decisions, like why you chose batch over streaming, not a long list of tools.
Do not add the project link if the repository is messy or unfinished. A weak repo is worse than none. Keep one version per target role, and cut anything you could not defend.

show.title: Edit ruthlessly
items: Link only a repo you are proud of

check.q: At staff level, what adds most value on a resume?
opts: A longer tool list
Scope and design decisions with scale
More skills than other candidates
Generic buzzwords
check.why: Staff roles are judged on scope and judgement. A tool list adds one more thing to defend and little signal.

work: Make a tailored version for each role type you apply to.
Add one design decision with its trade-off to your top role.
Check that your project repo is tidy before linking it.

title: Why a second offer lifts the first

beats.say: Why can a second job offer make your first one pay more?

show.text: One offer is a price. Two offers are a market.

beats.say: Think of selling your car. One buyer offers five thousand. You have no idea if that is fair. Then a second buyer offers six thousand. Now the first buyer knows you have choices. A competing offer is that second buyer. It is your strongest proof.
So try to land offers in the same week. If one company is slow, politely ask them to speed up. An offer that arrives after you have signed elsewhere helps nobody.

show.title: Line them up
items: Ask a slow company to speed up
A late offer is too late

beats.say: Then say the number that would make you accept, and give a reason. Stay friendly and specific. People like helping someone they enjoy talking to.

show.title: Make the ask
items: Name the number that gets a yes

check.q: Why is a competing offer such strong negotiation evidence?
opts: It proves you are in demand and have real alternatives
It lets you threaten the company
It means the first company must match it exactly
check.why: It shows the market value of your skills and that you can walk away, without needing any threat. Companies are not obliged to match it, but it makes your request credible.

work: When you start interviewing, try to schedule final rounds at several companies in the same two weeks.
Tell a slower company politely that you have another deadline and ask if they can speed up.
Write down the number that would make you accept and the one-sentence reason for it.

title: Comparing offers over four years

beats.say: Two offers. Which one pays more? It depends on which clock you use.
Offer A: two hundred thousand base, twenty thousand bonus, and four hundred thousand of stock that vests evenly. Year one is three hundred twenty thousand. Four years is one point two eight million.

Offer B: one ninety base, nineteen bonus, and four eighty of stock, vesting five, fifteen, forty, forty percent. Year one is just two thirty-three thousand. But four years is one point three one six million.
Vesting means stock becomes yours gradually. So add up all four years, then ask for the number that would make you accept.

check.q: Offer B pays less in year one but more over four years. What does that tell you?
opts: Offer B is always better
Back-loaded vesting pays most if you stay the full four years
Year one is the only number that matters
check.why: Back-loaded vesting shifts value to later years. It wins on a four-year total only if you stay long enough to collect it.

work: Build a simple sheet with one row per year for base, bonus and vested stock for each offer.
Ask each recruiter for the exact vesting schedule, not just the grant total.
Compare both the year-one number and the four-year total before you decide.

title: What can go wrong after a verbal yes

beats.say: What can go wrong between a verbal yes and your first day?

show.text: A handshake is not an offer.

beats.say: Verbal promises vanish. Before you resign, get the final offer in writing: base, bonus, share count, vesting schedule, start date, and sign-on terms. Offers can be pulled after a background check, and a resignation cannot be undone.

Read the equity fine print. A cliff means nothing vests until month twelve, so leaving at month eleven pays zero stock. Private shares may be impossible to sell. Options cost money to exercise. Sign-on bonuses often must be repaid if you leave early.

show.title: Fine print
items: Cliff: zero stock before month twelve
Private shares may not be sellable
Sign-on bonus may be clawed back

beats.say: Ask how the stock is valued: shares times today's price is real, a hoped-for future price is not.

check.q: You leave a company at month eleven of a four-year grant with a one-year cliff. How much stock have you earned?
opts: About eleven forty-eighths of it
A quarter of it
None of it
check.why: A cliff means nothing vests until the cliff date. Leave before month twelve and you keep none of that grant.

work: Ask for the written offer to list base, bonus, share count, vesting schedule with any cliff, and sign-on repayment terms.
Do not resign until you have signed and any background check is complete.
Ask what the company's current share price is based on and whether you can ever sell.

title: When the best offer is the wrong one

beats.say: When is the highest offer the wrong one to take?

show.text: Highest number is not best deal.

beats.say: Discount risky pay. Cash is worth face value. Private stock might be worth zero, so count it at a fraction. Compare offers on what you would realistically collect.

show.title: Count pay by how sure it is

beats.say: Level matters more than base. A higher level moves your pay band for every future raise and bonus, so negotiate level before dollars.
Never bluff about an offer you do not have. Recruiters talk, and a caught bluff can end the deal. Do not string along a company you would never join. Ask for your accept number, then accept it.

show.title: Keep your credibility
items: Do not string along a company you would decline

check.q: Which move usually has the biggest long-term effect on your pay?
opts: Negotiating a higher level before base salary
Asking for a slightly higher sign-on bonus
Mentioning a made-up competing offer
check.why: Level sets your pay band, so it compounds across raises and bonuses. A sign-on bonus is one-time, and bluffing risks the offer.

work: Rate each part of pay by how certain it is, then compare offers on the discounted total.
Ask each company which level the offer is for and what the pay band is for it.
Decide your accept number in advance, and take the deal if they meet it.

title: Why practice never really ends

beats.say: Why do pianists still play scales after ten years? Because skill fades when you stop using it.
Interview skill works the same way. One SQL problem and one coding puzzle, twice a week, keeps your hands warm.
Now add a notebook. Every time you get something wrong, write it down. Your mistakes become a personal study guide, because they show exactly where you are weak.
And once a week, read how a real company solved a real problem, then write one question you would ask its engineer. That is how you stay current.

show.title: Weekly reading habit
items: Write one question for the author
That is how you stay current

check.q: Why keep a written list of what you got wrong?
opts: It shows exactly where you are weak
It makes the practice session longer
It replaces doing more problems
check.why: The list turns random mistakes into a map of your weak spots, so your next practice goes where it helps most.

work: Book two fixed practice slots in your calendar this week.
Start a simple mistakes list in a notes app.
Pick one company blog to read this week.

title: The two weekly habits, step by step

beats.say: What does a year of this habit actually add up to?

show.sub: what does it add up to?

beats.say: Two sessions a week, each with one SQL and one coding problem. That is four problems a week, and about two hundred a year. Each miss goes on a list: the problem, what you did wrong, and the fix.
A week later, redo every problem on the list. If you solve it cold, cross it off. If not, it stays.
Reading runs in parallel. One blog post a week from a company on your target list is fifty-two a year. After each, write one paragraph asking the author what they gave up, or what broke at scale.

check.q: You missed a SQL problem on Monday. What is the best next step?
opts: Log the cause and redo it cold a week later
Read the solution and move on
Skip SQL and do only coding problems
check.why: Redoing a missed problem after a gap tests whether you truly learned it, instead of just recognising the answer.

work: Create a miss list with columns for problem, cause and fix.
Put a redo day on your calendar one week after each miss.
Write your first author question after your next blog post.

title: Why practice sometimes fails

beats.say: Why do some people practice for months and still repeat the same mistakes?
Because they log the answer, not the cause. Writing used wrong join is useless. Write why you chose it, such as forgetting that a left join keeps unmatched rows. The cause is what you can fix.

nodes.label: Forgot left join keeps unmatched rows

beats.say: Other traps: only picking problems you already like, never redoing the misses, and skimming blog posts without writing anything. Reading feels like learning, but recall is what interviews test.
Also remember a blog shows the success story. Teams rarely publish what failed, so ask what they tried first.

check.q: Which miss-list entry is most useful?
opts: Wrong join on question 14
Forgot that a left join keeps unmatched rows, so check row counts
Need to practice joins more
check.why: It names the cause and a concrete fix. The others only restate that you were wrong or give a vague plan.

work: Rewrite your last three misses so each states a cause and a fix.
Deliberately pick one problem type you avoid each week.
Ask of every blog post: what did they try and drop first?

title: Is the habit worth the time?

beats.say: Is this habit worth three hours every week, and when is it not?
It pays off when interviews are coming within a year, or when your daily work no longer stretches you. The cost is small, and the return is steady recall plus fresh design ideas.
Choose blogs by fit. Pick companies whose scale matches the roles you want, and make your questions about trade-offs: what did they reject, what did it cost, and what would they change now?
If time is tight, trade volume for depth: fewer posts, plus a mock interview with a friend. And the paragraph doubles as your answer to how do you stay current.

show.title: When time is tight
items: Add a mock interview with a friend
The paragraph is your answer to staying current

check.q: What makes a blog-post question most useful for senior interviews?
opts: It asks which tools the company uses
It asks what they rejected, what it cost, and what they would change
It asks how big their team is
check.why: Senior interviews test trade-off thinking, and questions about rejected options and costs practise exactly that.

work: Choose three target companies whose scale matches your goal roles.
Rewrite your blog questions to focus on rejected options and costs.
Trim the habit to fit your real weekly time, and do a mock interview monthly.

title: Warm up before the final

beats.say: Would you run your first marathon on the day of the big race? Interviews work the same way.
Think of a football team. Before the cup final, they play friendly matches. Real opponents, real pressure, but losing costs almost nothing.
So start with two or three companies you would accept but do not love. That is your practice tier. Your nerves and timing settle there.
Then go for the companies you most want. Add a few stretch roles slightly above your level alongside, just to see how they feel.

show.title: What comes next
items: Target tier: the companies you most want
Stretch tier: slightly above your level

check.q: Why interview at companies that are not your first choice?
opts: To collect as many offers as possible
To get real interview practice at lower stakes
To avoid ever talking to your favourite companies
To prove you are overqualified
check.why: The practice tier gives real interview experience while a mistake costs little, so your timing and nerves are settled before the companies you want most.

work: List two or three companies you would accept but would not rank first.
Book those interviews before any target company.
Note after each one what rattled you.

title: The three tier schedule

beats.say: Why interview at a company you do not even want most? Because offers have deadlines, and timing is everything.
Weeks one and two: two or three practice companies. Real interviews, lower stakes. You learn your pace and fix your weak answers.
From week three, start your target tier, the companies you most want. Run stretch roles, slightly above your level, in parallel.
Then aim for final rounds within two or three weeks of each other. Offers land together, and each one becomes leverage on the others.

check.q: Why try to bring final rounds close together?
opts: So offers arrive at similar times and can be compared
So you can skip the practice tier
So recruiters stop calling
So you only prepare once

title: Five questions for every recruiter

beats.say: Which five questions stop an interview loop from ambushing you? Ask every recruiter, before you prepare anything.
First, how many rounds, and what is each one? Second, is AI assistance allowed, required or banned in each technical round? Rules can differ round by round.
Third, may you code in Python, Scala or either? Preparing in the wrong language costs you minutes you cannot spare in a live round.
Fourth, what is the level, and what is fixed salary, variable pay and equity? Offers only compare fairly with all three. Fifth, is there a take-home, and how is it reviewed?

check.why: Variable pay and equity can differ greatly between offers, so a single headline figure hides the real comparison.

title: Costs and limits of the ordering

beats.say: Is it ever wrong to practice on real companies? Yes, and the cost is worth knowing.
Companies often block reapplying for months. A burned target is gone for a while. That is why dream roles go second, after your timing settles.
Compressing finals into two or three weeks costs energy and prep time. Too many loops at once and each gets a thinner effort. Cap active loops at what you can truly prepare for.

show.title: Trade-offs of compressing
items: Cost: energy and prep per loop

beats.say: Skip the practice tier if you already interview regularly. And if one offer deadline arrives early, ask for an extension, citing your other processes.

show.title: When to bend the plan
items: Early deadline: ask for more time

check.q: When is skipping the practice tier most reasonable?
opts: When you have never interviewed
When you are already interviewing regularly and feel sharp
When you only have one target
When the target is your dream job
check.why: Practice exists to settle timing and nerves. If recent interviews have done that, the practice tier mostly costs time.
